summary: An internal memo describing the datacomputer from a user's point of view. It was planned as a special ARPANET node devoted to managing a very large shared database, with a single data language used to describe and request data. The first service offering is described, along with how users reach it through access methods.

plainLanguage.summary: A giant shared filing cabinet attached to the network. You talk to it in one special language that tells it what you want to store or fetch.

subtitle: A specialized network node for managing shared databases.

tldr.problem: Programs on different computers need to access and share large amounts of data efficiently, but moving entire datasets over narrow network links wastes bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: The datacomputer acts as a dedicated ARPANET node that stores data, accepts queries in a special data language, and returns only the requested subset of information.
tldr.outcome: Users can describe their data precisely once in the data language and retrieve exactly what they need, avoiding overload on slow connections.

facts.label: Shared data size
facts.value: Several trillion bits, at least one trillion on-line

today: RFC 219 is a 1971 design memo describing an early vision for a network-attached data management system. It remains a historical document outlining concepts that influenced later database and data management systems.

sections.title: The Datacomputer Concept
sections.content:
RFC 219 describes a design for the datacomputer, a specialized node on the ARPANET dedicated to managing a very large, shared database. It is conceived as a black box with a single interface: a data language that defines everything it can do.

The datacomputer is not a general-purpose computer. Its processor and storage are components of an integrated system, devoted entirely to data management. Users are programs running on other computers across the network, with widely varying capabilities and needs, yet all sharing the same data.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of a regular computer that does many things, the datacomputer is a specialist that only manages and shares data, so it is very good at that job.

sections.title: System Design and Organization
sections.content:
The datacomputer has two network ports: a high-speed port for local users (80 times faster) and a low-speed port for remote users. Data is separated from descriptions; data elements are named, typed and ordered according to a data description stored in the system.

A hierarchical naming scheme and access controls handle privacy and integrity. The system maintains redundant copies and journals to recover from errors. From the datacomputer's perspective, the entire network is a collection of data streams, each with an associated description allowing it to parse records into named, typed elements.
sections.plainLanguage: The system keeps two mail slots: a fast one for nearby visitors and a slow one for distant ones. It remembers what each piece of data is called and what it means.

sections.title: Data Structure and Access
sections.content:
The database contains files, which are named, physically distinct collections of data. A file directory records names, locations and attributes; each file has a file description that defines its organization. Files are organized as records containing named fields. Records are variable in format and size, and fields are variable in length.

The system maintains an index—conceptually lists of pointers to records with certain properties. For example, an index might point to all records where the STATE field equals MASSACHUSETTS. The system assigns a unique identifier to each record that maps to its location.
sections.plainLanguage: Data is filed like a collection of forms. Each form has named blanks (fields), and the system keeps a list of which forms match what you are looking for.

sections.title: Subsetting and Retrieval
sections.content:
The core challenge the datacomputer addresses is subsetting without examining the entire file. Users rarely need the whole file; they need a small relevant subset. This is critical for remote users on slow links to avoid overloading the narrow channel.

The system supports three basic file maintenance operations: add a field or record, delete a field or record, and replace a field or record. Boolean operations (AND, OR, NOT) allow complex queries. Logical and physical ordering of records is supported, and the user can describe precisely what data is of interest.
sections.plainLanguage: You tell the system exactly which forms you want, not by reading every page, but by describing what you are looking for. The system finds them and sends only those.
